title: Is This How AI Games Should Be Made?
author: Upbeat_Ad_6119
selftext:
https://i.redd.it/0x9s31s48r1i1.gif

I have built [Cineruption](https://nebitula.itch.io/cineruption) for Epic AI MegaJam 2026 in just 3 days, and I think I've done a pretty great job, at least in my personal opinion.

Yeah, it still has flaws regarding visuals, texts, level design, and guiding the player through the game, and especially the code (the game mechanics are not fully polished). It still needs a lot of work and a lot of polishing to make game feel complete, but I guess it's a pretty good submission for a game jam.

The reason why I'm posting this is that I want to get some feedback, any constructive criticism would help me, coz I'm not an game designer at all, I'm just putting things how I feel, and it hard to understand for me what people might like, and how much u should explain something to them (especially in puzzle games). But what's more important, I also want to talk a bit about AI gamedev and anti-AI stuff.

Well, I'm experimenting a lot with game art styles. If you check out my games, you'll definitely see a wide range of them. The only thing that's constant is that I'm trying to keep the visuals extremely minimalistic, built from primitive components and flavored with a lot of procedurally generated textures and shaders.

I'm really trying to avoid using too much AI-generated art, not because I'm against using it or because I'm afraid of AI hate. No, my reason is simple: I haven't been able to get results that I personally find appealing enough to use in my games. I know people do really amazing things in that direction, but I'm honestly pretty dumb when it comes to using AI for art. That's why I mostly lean towards visual languages that can be achieved through code.

Now, about this specific game. How did I achieve these visuals, if anyone is interested?

I used AI to draw two characters: the main character's spritesheets for 7–8 animations in total, and the second character with just 3 sprites.

I intentionally kept the number of sprites extremely low for two reasons:

1. I have no idea how to make AI do it better.
2. I don't really care if it looks slop for this specific game, because those flaws actually work quite well with the game's general art style.

Even the character's walking animation is anatomically wrong, but I actually like it more than a proper animation. I tried multiple times to generate a proper walk cycle, and even though the individual sprites looked okay, I just didn't like the result as much.

Everything else you see in this game is pure code: basic shapes, grain, patch textures, fire distortion, multiple different artifact and glitch shaders, and lights.

Even though AI-generated art in this game makes up less than 10% of the visuals, and even though it was made for an "AI" game jam, I'm sure there will still be a lot of anti-AI people telling me why this game shouldn't exist. And I really don't understand that.

The only things I hate regarding AI are copying other people's work, aggressively claiming that you've put a lot of effort into something when it's obviously generated with a single prompt, and not disclosing the use of AI. Although, regarding the last point, I can understand people who have stopped disclosing AI usage because they receive so much hate for it.

Everything else has the right to exist. Even totally low-effort, sloppy games. That's pretty okay for me.

You know who struggles the most because of anti-AI hate? Not the people who make games just for cash, not the people who clone existing games pixel by pixel, nope. It's the people who really care about their games and are trying to put their soul into them. Those are the people who struggle the most.

Even if they use a lot of AI, what's the problem with that? Someone could say, "AI devs generate slop games because they use AI." Well, it's not about AI; it's about experience. Nobody knows how to do everything properly on their first try. It takes a lot of time, so it's okay to let people experiment, try to do something, or learn something new.

Now, returning to the title of this post: **"Is This How AI Games Should Be Made?"**

Well, what do you think? The way how I'm working on my games, is this the right direction to take when creating games with AI? Could we find some common ground with anti-AI people in the near future and make them agree that AI is not ultimately bad? Or would this specific example still be considered low-effort slop?

But honestly, I also see a lot of problems on the other side. There are tons of low-effort games that don't offer any new experiences. And even though I don't personally care that much about it, I can understand why it might piss some people off. So I want to encourage AI devs to experiment a lot and try to put something of their own, something personal, into their games, rather than just making whatever AI suggests. And honestly, I see huge potential here. People are already creating really interesting, unique, and inspiring things.

I'm NOT claiming that my workflow is the ultimately correct approach. Nope, it's just how I do things. There are many different ways and approaches, and that's exactly what makes it interesting. The diversity of approaches is what makes this whole thing exciting. The only things we should have in common are a lot of experimentation and a lot of effort put into polishing the result.

I hate this polarization in game development, and this post definitely won't fix it. I might even end up getting hate from both sides. But my point is that things shouldn't be just black and white. We need to find some common ground and work towards compromises.

**I'd genuinely love to hear your thoughts, even if you completely disagree with me (just please stay polite). And please, feel free to criticize Cineruption itself if you have something more constructive to say than just "AI slop" or "Hire real artists".**

comments.author: KlutzyAd5743
comments.body: Agree largely with you and the game looks cute. I’m also trying to use Ai in a way that still looks like a somewhat original style and I think you’ve pulled that off, so well done! But I would put a much clearer disclosure on your Itch page. As you said yourself, people can tolerate Ai if they see the creator has put in an effort and a clear own taste or originality, AND clearly discloses it…

replies.author: Upbeat_Ad_6119
replies.body:
Well I was doing it for all my games, and once I tried without it, as long as u have disclosure in tags, its valid. But yeah your point is valid and I will put it there in description also..

But honestly I’m tired of how people react.. someone rated one of my games with 1 start with quote “I could appreciate the game more if actual artists were involved”, and u know what is funny here? There was not “art” in the game at all. The game was just complete procedurally drawn things like boxes and soft-bodies.. how even should I involve the artist here? There is no sense! Many of anti-ai is basically lacks any understanding of how things could be done and where for example is the line between code and art.

And yeah, thanks for your feedback, and I wish u luck in your experiments, keep doing it!

And yeh,

replies.author: KlutzyAd5743
replies.body: I think the sentiment will evolve and change as with everything Ai these days. Most solo devs and studios will be using it and the big ones already do. What is original and interesting will become more important in my view
